description: How Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika reforms unleashed forces he could not control.
content_html:
Gorbachev Takes Power, 1985

Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the Communist Party on 11 March 1985. At 54 he was strikingly younger than his predecessors. Unlike Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko, he was fit, articulate, and deeply aware that the Soviet Union faced a serious systemic crisis: a stagnant economy, a demoralised population, and a military bogged down in Afghanistan.

Gorbachev did not intend to dismantle the Soviet Union. He wanted to save it. He believed the Soviet system was fundamentally sound but had been corrupted by Stalinist bureaucracy and Brezhnev-era stagnation. His goal was to make communism work better — not to replace it with capitalism or multi-party democracy. This misjudgement of what was needed would prove fateful.

Key Fact

Gorbachev wanted to reform and save the Soviet system, not destroy it. His twin reform programmes — glasnost and perestroika — were intended to modernise socialism. Instead, they unleashed political forces that the Soviet system could not contain.

Glasnost: Openness

Glasnost (openness) relaxed censorship and allowed unprecedented public discussion of Soviet problems, history and corruption. Previously banned books were published; newspapers began criticising government policies; television showed the reality of Afghanistan rather than propaganda victories; the crimes of Stalinism were discussed openly for the first time since the Khrushchev Thaw.

A pivotal moment for glasnost was the explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine on 26 April 1986. The Soviet government initially tried to conceal the accident and its scale, but glasnost made this impossible. Journalists and officials reported the truth; the government was forced to evacuate entire towns and acknowledge the scale of the disaster. Chernobyl became a symbol of Soviet institutional failure — the gap between official claims of technological achievement and the reality of a crumbling infrastructure.

Perestroika (restructuring) was Gorbachev's attempt to reform the Soviet economic system. It introduced limited market mechanisms: state enterprises were given more autonomy, cooperatives and small private businesses were permitted, and some price controls were relaxed. Politically, perestroika included a degree of democratisation: competitive elections were introduced for seats in a new parliament (the Congress of People's Deputies), held in March 1989.

Perestroika created more problems than it solved. The relaxation of price controls caused inflation; the partial introduction of market forces disrupted existing supply chains without creating new ones; state enterprises, freed from some controls, raised wages without increasing productivity. Economic output fell in many sectors. Rather than renewing Soviet socialism, perestroika destabilised it.

International Relations: The INF Treaty

One area where Gorbachev achieved genuine success was foreign policy. He recognised that the arms race was economically ruinous and that the Afghan War must end. He developed a personal rapport with US President Reagan and in December 1987 signed the INF Treaty, which eliminated an entire category of nuclear weapons (intermediate-range missiles) — the first arms control agreement actually to reduce nuclear stockpiles rather than merely cap their growth.

Soviet troops completed their withdrawal from Afghanistan in February 1989 — a tacit admission that the war had been a mistake. Gorbachev also announced that the Brezhnev Doctrine was effectively dead: Eastern European states would not be propped up by Soviet military force. This announcement — sometimes called the “Sinatra Doctrine” by Gorbachev's spokesman — opened the door to the revolutions of 1989.

Key Fact

The INF Treaty (December 1987) was the first US–Soviet agreement to actually eliminate nuclear weapons rather than cap their numbers. It marked the effective end of the Second Cold War and demonstrated that Gorbachev was a different kind of Soviet leader willing to make real concessions.

The fundamental problem with Gorbachev's reforms was that they were politically revolutionary but economically confused. Glasnost allowed public exposure of Soviet failures — corruption, environmental disasters, the Afghan War — without providing the improved material conditions that might have built public support for the system. As people spoke more freely, they began expressing not just demands for better management of socialism but desires for genuine political freedom and, in the national republics, for independence.

Conservative party officials and KGB elements feared the pace of change and blamed Gorbachev for destabilising the state. Reformers like Boris Yeltsin felt change was too slow and too limited. Gorbachev found himself squeezed between two forces he had inadvertently created: a conservative backlash and a democratic movement he could not satisfy without abandoning the party's monopoly on power. By 1990–91 the system he had tried to save was visibly disintegrating.
exam_tip_html: A common mistake on Gorbachev is to treat glasnost and perestroika as deliberate steps towards ending the Soviet Union. Make clear that Gorbachev’s intention was to save and reform socialism, not replace it. For ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions, the unintended consequences of reform (rising nationalism, economic disruption, loss of party control) are what examiners want to see. For the 16-mark Period Essay, remember to weigh factors: glasnost allowed freedom but perestroika caused economic chaos — which was more destabilising?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gorbachev became General Secretary in March 1985, intending to reform and save the Soviet system. His twin programmes were glasnost (openness, relaxing censorship) and perestroika (restructuring the economy and introducing limited elections).
  • Chernobyl (April 1986) became a symbol of Soviet institutional failure; the INF Treaty (December 1987) eliminated a class of nuclear weapons and marked the end of the Second Cold War.
  • Glasnost encouraged public criticism that grew beyond Gorbachev’s control; perestroika disrupted the economy without creating prosperity. By 1990 the reforms had unleashed forces — nationalist, democratic and conservative — that were pulling the USSR apart.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Gorbachev’s policy of glasnost.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: censorship was relaxed and previously banned books and articles were published; media could discuss Soviet failures and corruption; public debate about Stalinist crimes was permitted; the Chernobyl disaster could not be concealed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of perestroika as introduced by Gorbachev from 1986.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: state enterprises were given more autonomy and some market mechanisms were introduced; small private businesses and cooperatives were permitted; a new parliament (Congress of People's Deputies) was established with competitive elections in March 1989; price controls were partially relaxed, causing inflation.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Chernobyl disaster of 1986 for the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Key consequences: the disaster exposed the gap between official Soviet claims of technological achievement and the reality of a failing infrastructure; glasnost made it impossible to conceal the scale of the disaster; it undermined public confidence in the Soviet system; it reinforced Gorbachev's case that radical reform was necessary.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point, no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the INF Treaty of 1987 for relations between the Soviet Union and the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: first agreement to eliminate rather than cap nuclear weapons; ended the Second Cold War tensions; demonstrated Gorbachev was a different kind of Soviet leader. Over time: opened the door to further arms reductions; contributed to Eastern European revolutions of 1989 by signalling the USSR would not use force to defend regimes; marked the practical end of the Cold War.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Gorbachev’s reforms:

“Glasnost was more important than perestroika in destabilising the Soviet Union.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: glasnost allowed public exposure of Soviet failures, corruption and the Afghan War; it enabled nationalist and democratic movements to organise and speak openly; exposure of Stalinist crimes undermined the party's legitimacy; Chernobyl and Afghanistan coverage eroded trust.

Disagreement: perestroika directly disrupted the economy by dismantling central planning without replacing it with an effective market; rising inflation, supply chain disruption and falling output created genuine material grievances; democratisation through the Congress of People's Deputies gave a platform to political opposition.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was glasnost the main reason for the problems facing the Soviet Union by 1990? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For glasnost: enabled nationalist movements, democratic opposition, public criticism of party; gave platform to Yeltsin and others; exposed institutional failures including Chernobyl and Afghan War.

Alternative factors: long-term economic stagnation predating Gorbachev; perestroika's failure to deliver prosperity while disrupting supply chains; nationalities problem in republics seeking independence; conservative coup plotters undermining reform; external factors (US military pressure, oil price falls reducing Soviet revenue).

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple factors, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

knowledge_checks.q: Which nuclear disaster in April 1986 became a symbol of Soviet institutional failure under glasnost?
The INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated an entire class of _____ nuclear missiles.
Gorbachev's policy of economic restructuring was called _____.
Match each Gorbachev policy to its description:
right: Relaxation of censorship and openness of public debate
Economic restructuring with limited market mechanisms

flashcard_questions.q: When did Gorbachev become General Secretary?
What was Gorbachev's intention with glasnost and perestroika?
flashcard_questions.a: To reform and save the Soviet system, not destroy it.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Chernobyl nuclear disaster occur?
What did the INF Treaty (December 1987) achieve?
flashcard_questions.a: Eliminated intermediate-range nuclear missiles — the first agreement to reduce, not just cap, nuclear stockpiles.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Soviet forces complete their withdrawal from Afghanistan?

flashcard_questions.a: Gorbachev's informal abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine, signalling Eastern European states could choose their own path.

flashcard_questions.q: The Congress of People's Deputies was established with competitive elections in which year?
What economic problem did perestroika's partial price liberalisation cause?
Who was the reformist Soviet politician who eventually clashed with Gorbachev and led Russia?
What US president did Gorbachev develop a personal rapport with and sign the INF Treaty with?

glossary_terms.definition: General Secretary of the Communist Party from March 1985 and last leader of the Soviet Union, whose reform programmes of glasnost and perestroika unintentionally accelerated the USSR's collapse.
The policy of openness introduced by Gorbachev from 1986, which relaxed censorship and allowed greater freedom of expression and public debate.
The policy of economic and political restructuring introduced by Gorbachev from 1986, intended to modernise the Soviet economy through limited market mechanisms.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty signed by the USA and USSR in December 1987, eliminating an entire category of nuclear weapons.
The Soviet nuclear power station in Ukraine that exploded on 26 April 1986, becoming a symbol of Soviet institutional failure and a crisis for Gorbachev's glasnost policy.
The informal name for Gorbachev's abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine, signalling that Eastern European states would not be held in the Soviet bloc by military force.
